speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
I must take issue with the proposition as laid down by the Minister of Railways to-day. He says this is for a local branch, for a small portion of the road, that it is not a part of any general plan. I say we should have a statement here to-day giving us a general plan, showing how the government propose to deal with the transcontinental railway proposition. He has opened wide the door for assistance, and every railroad running through a new country where there are settlers desiring railroad facilities, is bound to be assisted by the government. His statement went that far. He said : Here is a new country, available for settlement, there are settlers in it, and the government feel bound to assist this road. Welt, if they say that in this case, they must say it in all cases ; and they should have been prepared to say today whether this proposition to aid a transcontinental road is to be followed next week by another proposition to aid the Grand Trunk Pacific road. We have no statement whatever in that respect. Now, when the government came down to the House with this proposition, they were bound to come prepared to state their general policy on the transcontinental railway question. They have not done it. I cannot vote for a proposition of this kind. For what has happened ? This railway running from Port Arthur to Winnipeg in the west heretofore has been very largely bonused by the people of this country. When the first portion of this railway was considered in thiq House, I took the position then that if public money was to be put into a road, it should be a government owned' railway, for the only way to solve the railway problem is for the government to own a road from one ocean to the other, a road controlled by the people, and its ratios regulated by the people in such a way that every other road will have to live up to that standard. They should have done that long ago, they should have done that with the Rainy River road, and the minister said Mr. FOWLER.
he had some idea of it in his mind, but he said at the time : This is only a small section, let this go through. Now comes along another section, and he says : We must take this as part of a proposition, let it go through. The country expects something very different from the government. They expect that the government should outline its policy in regard to transcontinetal railways. The only thing to do if they are putting in public money is to build a government road. Hon. gentlemen have heard a good deal in this House about a government owned railway, and they have heard a great deal from their supporters. Some years ago only a few of us took that view, but now there is a growing demand in the country for a government owned railway. This is one of the signs of the times. There are hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House who said that free trade was bound to live for ever, and that the protectionist proposition was not a policy which would last. To-day
Order.

I am only mentioning the point in illustration-England is in a ferment over the trade question, and the bulk of the leading English statesmen in England are beginning to see that the time has come for revision of their policy and are becoming protectionists.
ill-. COWAN. You have not read this morning's papers.

Yes, I have. The same thing is happening in connection with the railway question. The people are coming rapidly to the opinion that if the national credit is to be given towards the building of a trans-continental railway the government should build a road which should be owned and controlled by the people. Instead of that, we are giving our money for a railway controlled by private parties. This is not good policy, and it is not in line with what the people expect. What follows V It follows as sure as night follows day that next week or the week after, another proposition will be introduced into the House providing for an immense bonus, probably a land grant, or an immense guarantee to the Grand Trunk Pacific. Where is all this to end ? The door is open wide and the policy has been set forth as the policy of tlie government that if there is a new country with settlers in it and a railway is desired the country must build that railway.
I cannot vote for a proposition based upon that principle. The hon. minister says : We are committing ourselves to nothing. We are committing ourselves to a great deal. In the first place we are guaranteeing over $9,000,000 of money. It is a commitment which will affect the credit of the country more or less, and if there is to be a commitment to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway of the same kind that will affect the

credit of tlie country also. We are rapidly dissipating tlie credit of tlie country in building railways for private corporations. 1 do not think the feeling of this country to-day is in favour of any such policy. The feeling of the country to-day, and lion, gentlemen will find it out when the voice of the people is heard, is against this system of bouusing railways owned by private individuals. I have not the slightest objection to that country having a railway. 1 believe the men who are seeking aid under this proposition are enterprising men and that they are opening up the country, but they are opening up the country for their own benefit rather than for the benefit of the country. The hon. minister says that we are practically giving nothing away. Do you know what backing this note of the Canadian Northern Railway Company is worth V We are told that it will enable them to borrow money for 3 per cent. If they had to go upon the open market and borrow it tliey would probably have to pay 6 per cent, so that it is worth $30,000 a year on each million, or $270,000 a year. It is practically a perpetual bonus to this enterprise. We are giving this road a quarter of a million annually and there is no prospect of getting anything in return. The hon. minister says that we are going to control the rates. How far have we controlled rates up to the present time 7 It is true something lias been secured by the bargain which the province of Manitoba made with this railway company. They have reduced the rates in a measure, but not in such a way ns they should have been reduced. For one thing there should have; been a maximum freight rate provided for" in this agreement, and most of all a maximum passenger rate should have been put in. That is where you get control of railways. We have to deal with the Canadian Pacific Railway, we may have to deal with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, and other roads may grow up. The Canadian Northern is one of them. Every one of these roads could be absolutely controlled by the competition of a government railway or by stipulating with these roads the passenger and freight rates which should be charged upon them. Is anything of that kind proposed in these resolutions V Nothing of the kind. We have had no great results from what was promised in the past in the way of taking control of these railways and their rates. We have had no satisfactory results from the amount of money we have expended and we are going on and spending millions and millions on our terminals, on improving lake and river navigation, on improving the seaports, because they say the nation must do this work. What is the good of spending all that money on lake navigation, on the canals, and oil' ocean terminals if we have no control over railways ? The only way to have complete control is by having at least one government owned railway. We are spending enough money on all of these different propositions to build a government road from one ocean to the other. Why should we not have it ? Why should not the Intercolonial Railway be extended to the Pacific ocean ? Why should not all this money that the people are putting up be put into a proposition in support of a railway owned and controlled by the people ? The money is being frittered away. The problem is not being solved, but it is being complicated by such a proposition as the one which we have before us now. It makes it harder to control these railways and eventually to settle the transportation problem. I stand in my place in this House and I tell the government that the people of this country are opposed to this system of bouusing railways. This bonusing proposition which is presented here to-day is very much milder than similar propositions in the past, as there is no land grant, there is no grant of money, and there is some regulation in regard to freight rates, but I submit that though the proposition is presented in a modified form to-day, the sentiment of the people is against the bonusing of private owned railways in this country and lion, gentlemen will find it out. 1 am willing to take my risk, whatever it may be, in standing by that policy and of saying that any money that we put into a trans continental line ought to be put into a railway owned and controlled by the government and made the complement of the lake and river navigation system that we are supposed to be building up. What is the use of paying immense sums in improving mu-seaports, in lighting the St. Lawrence, in the canals, in improving river navigation and lake navigation and in providing terminals on the lakes, if we cannot substantially control the railways that feed these ports ? I will allow the hon. members from the North-west Territories to deal with that question. They have their constituents to face, and the wish of the people of the North-west Territories agrees altogether with what the people of eastern Canada think, that the time has come to stop the bonusing of railways and to put all this money into a government railway. I do not: wish to go into the details of this measure. The hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) pointed out, here, to-day, that the greatest care ought to be taken as to the standard of the road and as to the way in which it is built. The road can be overcapitalized. It might be constructed in a way that would interfere with its working afterwards. These minor details and everything of that character should be do seiy looked into, but I shall not speak of that now so much as in regard to the fact that the government are building a railway which they are not going to control, and they are doing it in such a way that they are not working out a trans-continental

system, in such a way that it does not justify the national expenditure on lake terminals, sea terminals and lake and river navigation, and they are doing it in spite of the well expressed opinion of the people that the day has come to end this subsidizing of private owned railways.

Mr. Chairman, I do not want to enter into a general discussion of this measure, but I wish to say that when the final discussion takes place on the Bill I hope that the government will be prepared to make a clear explanation as to tlveir policy in regard to a trans-continental line. There is no doubt that public opinion, in the province of Quebec at least, and indeed in the whole of Canada-until the moment that notice of these resolutions was given-lay in the direction, that if tjie money of the people of Canada was required to aid any large railway enterprise in the west, it was to include a through transcontinental railway which would not only develop the grain traffic of the west, but would connect the east and the west and develop the general traffic of Canada. 1 fear that the passage of these resolutions and the Bill which will be based upon them, will tend to prevent the adoption of a general scheme for a transcontinental line.
A government line.

I do not say a government line. I fear, though I hope it will not, that it will render more difficult the early construction of any transcontinental line such as the Grand Trunk Pacific or any other scheme that may be favoured by parliament. The moment this line is being operated it will cover the more profitable trade of the country for the present, because there is no doubt that the transportation of grain from the North-west to Lake Superior is the most profitable part of the business now, and therefore when a new line comes and finds itself deprived of a good share of that traffic it will be less disposed to build a line from Lake Superior to Quebec and the maritime provinces. 1 trust that the government have studied the situation in this light, and that when this Bill is brought before the House they will make a declaration of thein policy and assure us of the eastern provinces, that the building of the road from Winnipeg to Quebec and the maritime provinces through the northern portions of Ontario and Quebec will not be jeopardized by this scheme.
On the general question of our railway policy, although I do not go so far as my hon. friend from East York (Mr. Maclean) there is no doubt there is a growing feeling in Canada that it is time to put an end to our railway policy of the past. No country in the world is so greatly in need of railways as Canada. There is no country in the world where railways mean so much for the future of the country both from a commercial and from a political point of Mr. MACLEAN.
view, and at the same time there is no country in the world where railways have been built with so little care as to their future consequences to the people. We have spent more money on our railways, in proportion to our population, than the people of any other nation, and there is less probability that we shall have a return from them, than is the case with any other nation. I had hoped from the declaration made byi the Minister of Finance last session, when I brought the subject before the House in the debate on the address, that the government would be able to advise us this session, and give us some hope that there would be a change in our railway policy. I admit that in these resolutions there is a change, and a change for the better. This way of dealing with the Canadian Northern Railway is far better than the system of the past under which we simply squandered the money of the jmople without any expectation of a return from it. But at the same time this change is not sufficient. We should go more fully into the matter and we should study the railway policy of other nations which have better solved the problem than we have, or that the people in England and the United States have. In continental Europe they are greatly in advance of England and the United States and Canada so far as their railway policy is concerned. , With the exception of Germany they do not go so far as ownership and operation by the government, and I think that is wise because where they have tried it they have found it a failure. But they have adopted a mixed system by which the state retains the ownership of the railway, the right of property in the railway, but gives the operation of it for a certain number of years to private companies under the control of the state. The title which is given to the company is only a lease of power, for the operation of the road under the supervision of the government, and the aid given to the railway is only a guarantee of interest.
With what result has that been worked out ?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: With splendid results so far as France, Belgium and Holland are concerned.
My information is quite the other way.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: In France and Holland especially they have tried different systems, and if the minister studies the question he will find that the mixed system which they have adopted of late has largely succeeded.

My hon. friend. (Mr. Bourassa) must have observed that the French government had a very large deficit last year,

and tliat the greater part of that was due to the loss on the operation of their railways under the system that he refers to.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The hon. Minister of Railways is strengthening my contention because the deficit was on the state owned and state operated railways.
Under the system the hon. gentleman refers to.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I may tell the minister that there are two systems; in fact there are three systems going on together in France. At first they gave charters to companies with permanent powers such as we are doing, and there are only a few small lines which remain under that system. Under the second system they went to the other extreme as they generally do there, and they had state owned and state controlled railways, and a certain number of railways remain in that condition at the present day.
You mean state operated.

Yes. Then they constituted the six great companies with which they entered into an agreement in 1857. Of course political events in France had some effect on the railway policj- and created some disturbance. For example, after the revolution of 1848 sonde of the smaller companies having failed, the government extended their state operated system. They took the Charente $nd Vendee systems and after that, during the empire, they more or less balanced the three systems together. After the war of 1870, there was, of course, a great disturbance in the operation of their railways, primarily because of the annexation of Alsace and Lorraine, which deprived some of the railway companies of a part of their system. After more or less dis turbance, in 1879, the French government under Mr. d6 Freycinet, tried to extend the state operated system and they changed their agreements with the six great companies. They took over a part of their system and it is upon that state owned and operated system that the deficits have occurred every year. But upon the system belonging to the six great companies which are operated under the dual system there has been no deficit.

May it not be, that the reason the state operated railways do not pay is that the best railways were taken by the companies, and the worst left to the state ? It has been stated by some writers on the subject in the magazines, that where there is a mixed system of state owned and company owned railways, the state always get the heavy end of the plank.

In theory that is right, but the-state owned system of France was born before the agreement with the six companies Under the arrangement of
1879, made by Mr. De Freycinet, part of the system of these great companies was annexed to the state system, but that went on for only four years, and in the general revision of 1883, the state deprived itself of these lines which it had annexed in 1879, and concluded an arrangement with the six great companies by which they handed back these parts that they had taken in 1879.
Now, I am ready to admit with the Minister of Railways and Canals that over some Parts of the railway system of France the arrangement has not worked so well as over other parts. But if you go into a careful analysis of the system you will find-That wherever there is a large deficit it is due to the fact that the government forced the companies to build certain lines that were entirely unprofitable. That was done through political pressure, and the deficit is due to causes entirely apart from the system itself. They also adopted a very peculiar policy-and it is not a policy I would recommend-but at that time they had reason to do it. They classified the railways into two systems, the old system and the new system. They guaranteed the interest on the new system, and, in order to make it up, they forced a part of the profits of the old system to be applied on the new system. This caused some disturbance, and they have now done away with that part of the system, because it' is no mbre needed. If the hon. minister would go into a study of the French state operated railways, he would find that everywhere there is a deficit upon them. That system is not a success, and the people of France know that it is not, though they probably continue it for the same reason that we continue the Intercolonial Railway. But leaving aside the state-operated railways, which consist of only about 2,500 kilometers, while the systems of the great companies consist of 26,000 kilometres, the hon. gentleman will find that the general system, as it was adopted in 1857, and renewed by the last agreement of 1883, is not only successful, but is the one feature of French politics which is the most hopeful, so far as finance is concerned. The prospects of the railways, after an experience of forty-three years, are such that when the leases expire in 1956, instead of being a burden on the French people and increasing their debt, they will probably be the means of reducing the debt of the French people by an immense figure. In fact, independent of the state operated railways, and independent of those parts of the lines which have been built and operated under special circumstances, the amount of interest paid by the French government on what we may call the ideal system is diminishing every year ; and, after ninety-nine years, that is in 1956, the whole system will go back to the French government. But their intention is not to operate the railways at the end of the leases, but to lease them over again on such conditions as they will be abld to impose,



which at tliat time will probably be more favourable than the present conditions, because of the increase of population and trade and the better management of the system.
There is no general railway law in France. The railways are operated under a kind of agreement, a model schedule, which is modified according to special circumstances. There are dispositions of the schedule giving the same powers of control to the government as we have here, and .power to revise the rates at different periods. There are other powers also. For example, the government would have the right to take possession of the railways at any time during the lease, and put an end to the lease.
On the state-owned and state-operated railways of Germany, there were at first decreases of the rates, and that is one of the dangers of state operated railways. These decreases were too great. At first they were pleasing to the people, but the government came to the conclusion that they were going to bankrupt the system, and they had to impose higher rates, which, of course, caused a great deal of discussion. Holland formerly operated its own railways, but finally adopted the French system, and now has state owned railways operated by chartered companies under special agreement. Germany has kept state owned and state operated railways to a large extent, in spite of the inconvenience of the system, for purely military reasons, which do not exist here. I did not intend to go so fully into this *question ; but I have given these explanations because I think the time lias come when we should study seriously our railway policy. We shall not effect any improvement by putting off the question from year to year! Every charter and every aid we grant to a railway company to-day is so much of the national wealth of the country being given away to private individuals without any hope of return ; and the time has certainly come when we should have a more intelligent and conservative policy for the people of Canada in railway matters.

On the general question of providing for an extension of railway accommodation in the particular parts of the country through which these proposed lines are to'run, I think there can be, and there Is actually and practically, no contrary opinion. Upon that general question I do not intend at the present time to add anything to what I have said to this House on previous occasions. I think, too, with the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat, that the present proposition is very far in advance of any other railway proposition ever presented to this House, and upon this fact I sincerely congratulate the hon. gentlemen who occupy the treasury benches. 1 do not know, however, whether these resolutions are as good as they possibly might be made. X think this parliament is in duty
bound at the present time to make for the people the very best possible bargain with these railway promoters and contractors, the Canadian Northern Railway Company. A number of very good suggestions have been made to the hon. Minister of Railways and Canals by the hon. leader of the opposition and other members of the House this afternoon. There is one, however, wbicli has not been made, and which I am going to make. Personally I favour the principle so consistently and enthusiastically championed by the hon. member for East York (Mr. Maclean)-the principle of government ownership and operation of railways. Still, I do not feel that at present I can go with him the full length of demanding that the government shall at once commence to apply that principle in this country. I know, and I think lie knows and recognizes, that to-day there is not in this House a majority of members in favour of the immediate application of that principle ; and I very much question whether there will be found throughout the country a majority of the people in favour of its immediate application. At the same time. I agree with him that the feeling in favour of the principle Is growing, and growing with considerable rapidity, and I think it would be well to have in the proposed contract a clause which would enable the government at some future time, when the majority of the people of the country believe in the application of that principle, and when they will elect to this House a majority of members in favour of its immediate application, to take over on fair and reasonable terms the lines which we are at present proposing to aid and have constructed. There was another suggestion, which I consider a very good and very essential one, made by the hon. member for East York ; that is, that there should be put in this contract a provision for maximum rates, so that the people along the lines to be constructed shall know definitely and distinctly what advantage they are to receive in return for what the public is doing for this company. For these reasons, to allow of time to frame some further provisions, and to further perfect the bargain which has been already agreed upon to some extent between the government and the railway company, I would concur in the suggestion of the hon. leader of the opposition. that the question should not be pressed to a conclusion at the present time, but that further time be given for consideration.

I understand that it is not the intention of the hon. minister to conclude the discussion on this subject to-day, but that in probably a week or ten days the matter will be again before the House. I think that the hon. minister should then bring down at least a rough draught of the actual contract to be entered into with this company and also a copy of the mortgage to be given by it to the gov-

ernment. In the transaction which took place between this company and the Manitoba government, 1 think that the mortgage was actually brought before the House and discussed. However, these are matters which can be discussed later on as well as the rates of freight and the question of government ownership. I may say, however, that the majority of the people of the west are rather sorry that the dream of the hon. minister did not come true, and that when he woke up, he did not go on and carry that beautiful dream into practical effect.
I do not think he is awake yet.

But the giving of assistance to this road need not prevent the government front constructing at any time a road of its own. I do not believe that there is one mile of the road aided by this Bill which will not pay from the start. From Lake Superior to Edmonton, it will be a paying road every day it runs. But there are some things we ought to carefully see to, judging by our experience in the past. In my opinion the government should employ an engineer and some assistants, whose duty it would be to keep continually going over the road and look after the manner of construction. The Canadian Pacific Railway, although it has been built over twenty years, was so imperfectly constructed that this year, as is pointed out in the Winnipeg papers, in addition to the ordinary section men employed by the company, Messrs. Foley-Larson Company have three thousand men actually at work putting that line into shape between Winnipeg and Port Arthur. It is a well-known fact also that the Crow's Nest road, which was assisted by this government, will practically have to be rebuilt from Lethbridge into the Mountains. The cuts through the mud hills are in such a shape that it will cost as much to build a new road as to repair the old one. Therefore, I would urge on the government and the hon. minister that competent men should be employed to supervise the construction of the road and see that the grading and bridges and terminals are properly constructed. This company say that they will only have 5 per cent of a grade, but how they can cross the Saskatchewan river five times, how they can lay five bridges across the Saskatchewan and go up and down the hills leading to and from those bridges, without a steeper gradient than .5 per cent, is an engineering problem I would not like to have to solve. There is another phase of the question to which I would call attention. When the Canadian Pacific Railway was built-its main line as well as its branches-and when the Crow's Nest road was built, the treatment of the men was such as to bring disgrace on the Dominion. Every one must recollect that when in 1897 the Crow's Nest road was under construction, telegrams were sent abroad of such a nature as forced 1381
the right hon. the First Minister to take action. Government officers should be put on the road to see that the men are paid proper wages and fairly treated. Of course if there should be such a crop in Manitoba and the west as we had last year, there will be no difficulty on the point of wages paid, except this : In the case of the Crow's Nest road, the men were not givan proper food, the camps were not properly constructed, the bedding was not what it should be, there was not sufficient accommodation for the men, but worse than that, the men who were hired at Winnipeg to go to the work, were charged a high rate of transport to get there and another high rate to get back, and were charged besides other excessive charges, so that all a man could, earn was about $13 per month net. I sent out myself on this very road a large number of Doukhobors, Galicians and others, who had worked full time, and the poor men, when they had paid the charges for transport, and the fees of a doctor, whom they never saw, at the rate of $1 per month, and $3 per sack for flour, had their pay reduced down to the minimum. Thirteen dollars or thirteen fifty per month was about all they could make.
The construction of this road should be made the means of colonizing the prairie. By the construction of the Northern Pacific and the Great Northern railways, the states of Minnesota and Dakota were settled, but unfortunately the manner in which the Canadian Pacific Railway was built and its branches, the Manitoba and South-western and the Deloraine, so disgusted the men employed that they left the country. It is the duty of the government to see that the men employed are properly fed and housed, and not overcharged for their supplies or transport; and if that were done, I believe that we would get many good, hardy settlers in there to earn a few dollars, who would afterwards settle along the prairie. But the company should not be allowed to go to Minneapolis, Duluth and Chicago and hire a lot of Italians under the Padrone system, at perhaps ninety cents per day, for this would do the country harm instead of good. Now is the time, whpu we are putting the company under certain obligations, to insist on fixing the conditions.
With regard to the equipment of the road, the hon. minister should state exactly what equipment it shall have per mile-what box cars, passenger and flat cars and engines, and the style of engines. It is well known that notwithstanding the fact that there are less engines per mile on the American roads to-day, they haul more than was hauled five or six years ago, because the engines are larger. We should have a statement as to what the equipment will be at the end of two, three or five years. The hon. minister says that it is not customary to have a road up to proper equipment during construction, but from the time the first

hundred miles on this road are built and in operation, there will be enough freight to yield a handsome profit. You cannot compare it to a new. road constructed over new territory, because the country will be settled just as quickly as the road is constructed. In fact, there are settlers in there now.
Another question is whether or not this is to be a great national highway. X do not think tliat it is necessary to decide that question just now. If the government should undertake to construct a great national highway, this road will not stand in the way, and they may use this road or not as they choose. They are given running power over it in one of the clauses. Any road may have running powers over it, but unfortunately I do not think that the terms on which running powers may be given to other roads are sufficiently well stated. The clause says they shall be given running powers on an equitable basis, but I believe that basis should be defined. If the Grand Trunk Railway or any other road wants to run over this road, the terms should be stated. I will not discuss that Manitoba bargain, nor another question which I think the minister probably overlooked, and that is the condition of that part of the Canadian Northern system which is merely leased, as I may say, from the Northern Pacific Railway. Three hundred and fifty-seven miles in the province of Manitoba were taken over .from the Northern Pacific Railway Company at $7,000,000, which calls for $210,000 to be paid annually. I do not know whether the minister had a copy of that deed before him in framing this mortgage. It is as well that he should have. They have not the fee of the road ; it is merely a leasehold, and it can be closed out in sixty days or ninety days, I am not sure which. I got the exact particulars from the president of the road. I think that this is a matter which should be looked into. As I said, I shall defer any further discussion of the matter until the contract itself is brought before the House.

As this seems to be an occasion for giving advice to the government, I prop se to offer such suggestions as occur to my mind. I would ask for some indulgence from the House in the matter, as I happen to represent a part of the country served by the railway proposed to be constructed. I would like to rather emphasize the importance of the proposition now before the House. There seems to me a tendency to belittle it as not being of the importance of a great transcontinental scheme. It is true, this is not as important as if it were part of a transcontinental scheme ; but allow me to say that it is of stupendous importance, not merely to the handful of people who are now in the country proposed to be served, nor merely to the thousands or hundreds of thousands who Mr. McCreary.
are shortly to occupy that country, but to the whole Dominion of Canada. The road is for the development of the Saskatchewan valley, and the Saskatchewan valley is the coming grainary of Canada, of North America and, possibly, of the world.
What about the Red River valley ?

The Red River valley is part of the great country of which the Saskatchewan valley is very much the larger part. The part of that great wheat growing area of the North-west which, long ago, was called the fertile belt, and which includes the valleys of the Red River and the Saskatchewan, is the part of the country to which Canada must look for its future development in wealth and population. There, and there only, have we the area of fertility suitable for the growth of population and the production of wealth that will ever constitute this Canada a great country. So, I say, it is of the very highest importance, looked at from a national standpoint, first that such a road as this should be constructed, and. second that it should be constructed under proper conditions. I shall say nothing with regard to the amount of aid to be given, the manner in which that aid is to be given nor the security to be taken. I do not think we need quarrel about any or all of these three particulars. It does not matter so much to this country whether we guarantee the bonds to the amount of $10,000 a mile or $13,000 a mile ; it does not matter so much even if we have to pay the interest on these bonds. What does matter to us is the amount we shall have to pay for the service we get from the road. I have troubled the House and some of the committees on some other occasions on this subject, and I propose to trespass again and to emphasize the point that the rates to be charged on this railway for the service of the country through which it runs, and, even more, for the service of the whole country, is the important question in this connection. There seems to be an idea that the transportation question of Canada begins at Fort William and extends to Quebec. Allow me to say that Canada has no serious transportation question over that distance. Nature and what we have done in the past has, in very large measure, solved the transportation question over that distance, so that when grain comes east, once it reaches Fort William, there is then no question as to the transportation or the rates from that point to its ultimate market. Neither is there any serious question as to the transportation of manufactured articles going westward until Fort William is reached. The lake navigation and the railroads fulfil in great part the requirements. I do not say that improvement cannot still be made ; of course we admit that it can. We do not say that it is not

desirable ; of c urse it is. But wliat 1 say is that it is not of the stupendous importance of the transportation question over the distance from Fort William westward. I do not think 1 need dwell on the importance to the wheat producers of the west of the lowest possible rate for the hauling of their grain to the ultimate market which, as I said before, means the lowest possible rate for their grain from the wheat fields to Fort William-Beyond that point we need not concern ourselves very seriously. But, from the wheat fields to Fort William is where the toll is taken that keeps the Northwest settler poor and keeps this country back, and, in the legislation which this parliament passes and in the aid it chooses to give, that is the point we need to emphasize and keep in mind. Just let me say, for the purpose of emphasis that a difference of a cent a bushel on the grain rate from the wheat fields to Fort William makes a difference of half a million dollars on every 50,000,000 bushels of wheat exported.
Do you expect to have many crops of fifty millions of bushels for export?
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: We do, certainly. I am thankful to have my attention called to that point. AVe expect many times fifty million bushels, and we need, and we expect, a number of reductions in freight rates to the amount of one cent per bushel each. The fifty millions of bushels which we speak of as the export product last year was produced very largely-in fact it was altogether produced-in what we still call the RedRiver-Valley-Section of the North-west, that is the drainage area of the Red, Assiniboine and Q'Appelle rivers. That is the area which produce the 50,000,000 bushels. When you consider the sparse settlement throughout the greater part of that area, and take the total area from Grandview to Edmonton and beyond, I think you will agree that our present production is not a quarter, is not a fifth of the production that necessarily will occur when the country is settled all the way to Edmonton and beyond Ihrough the Saskatchewan valley.
The export quantity
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I wish to protest against the manner in which questions are being asked by members on the other side of the House. Questions have been asked by the Minister of Railways and Canals and by other members, but not a man on this side of the House knows what is being said. I think a little respect should be shown to the gentlemen on this side of the Hou.se, and when a question is asked it should be asked in such a manner that we can hear it and know what the answer is.
I was speaking-
Tell us what the minister asked you, and what your answer is.

I was speaking of the prospective increase in exports, and suggested that, taking the comparative areas and the prospects, our exports would certainly be increased five fold when the Saskatchewan valley was settled up as the Red river valley is now. The minister suggested that our exports would not increase proportionately. I would be very glad to believe that the population of Canada would increase to such an extent that our exports would not increase proportionately. But I for one do not see that there is anything in our present prospects to indicate that our exports will not be in proportion to our production. At any rate the question of transportation from the wheat fields to Fort William would remain the same, because our great increase of consuming population, aside from our producing population, would be naturally in eastern Canada. So the question of rates on grain would be just the same then as now, except that we would be paying out at both ends, that is, the eastern consumer would be paying as well as the western producer; whereas now it is the western producer and the consumer in the old country. But I do not want to dwell on that point, everybody understands that feature of the case.
The point I want to emphasize is that this is not a question which concerns alone the producers of wheat in the North-west, but that the eastern manufacturer, the eastern commercial man, is just as deeply interested in a low freight rate to the wheat fields of the west as the producer of wheat in the west is interested in a low freight rate to reach the markets of the world. The ultimate market for the manufacturers and commerce of eastern Canada is necessarily these wheat fields. It is there or it is nowhere. Either you are going to have increased manufactures because of your increased market there, or you are not going to have increased manufactures. Now, it is of just as much importance to you that you should have the lowest possible rate to place your manufactures in these wheat fields as it is that the western farmer should get his grain out at a low rate. The difference between a high rate and a low rate to the western farmer means a difference in his profits; but if you cannot get a rate that will enable you to get your manufactures into the west, you cannot manufacture at all, your throat is cut, you cannot do business.
Now, let me point out just how and where your throat is cut. It is a matter of notoriety that in western Canada the importations of United States machinery for agricultural purposes has increased in recent years far beyond the increase of our population. Your manufacturers of eastern Canada are not keeping pace with the increased

population of the west in their sales. Now, why is this ? There is no difference in the protective duty, and there is no difference in the freight rate over our eastern lines. The difference is because the manufacturing centres of the United States which supply those articles are situated so close to the Canadian boundary enjoy the lowest possible freight rates from the Atlantic coast; they are therefore able to put their products into our wheat fields at a rate that you in this end of the country cannot compete with under present circumstances. Not only is that so in heavy manufactures, but it is also so in heavy groceries. I have visited the cities of St. Paul and Minneapolis, and it must be borne in upon any Canadian who visits those cities that the trade of the Canadian North-west is one of the principal reasons for the great prosperity of those cities. This is recognized by the people there, they look upon the North-west of Canada as their meat. They are growing with its growth, they are prospering with its prosperity, and they expect to continue to do so. And unless you can improve the freight rates which at present keep you .out of the North-west market, they are going to continue to prosper and grow, and you are going to continue to stand still, as you have done to a very large extent in the past.
What is true of St. Paul and Minneapolis in regard to our North-west is just as true in regard to Spokane in connection with the Kootenay mining district in British Columbia. Spokane papers are published with that in view, the commercial houses are run with that end in view, for the reason that Spokane gets a low freight rate by reason of railway competition. It is close to the Canadian border, and the Canadian Pacific Railway charges a high freight rate from the east. No matter how high you put your duty it is calculated into the freight rates, and you get no benefit from it. I say the cities of Spokane and St. Paul have grown within the past few years as no cities in Canada have done, and their growth has been principally, within very recent years, because of the growth and development of the adjoining North-west of Canada. The reason of that is because they have had the benefit of freight rates which our eastern manufacturers have not got, and when this parliament and this government propose to do anything in the way of increasing railway facilities in that country, it is their first duty to meet that case and see that railroad rates are cut, and cut to the bone. And why not V If we are guaranteeing the bonds of a railroad company to the amount that will be required to build and equip that railroad, as I understand we are doing on this occasion-and very properly I believe-then there is every reason why we should take into consideration the necessities of our trade in the development of our country, and place Mr. OLIVER.
the rates on such a basis as will ensure our own markets for our own people.
It has been suggested, when I have mentioned this matter before, that provision is made in these resolutions for a control of rates over this proposed railway. I read :
6. Resolved. That the rates and tolls to be charged tor the transfer and carriage of freight and passengers upon the lines of railway so aided and upon the lines owned by the Canadian Northern Railway shall he under the control of the Governor in Council or of such authority, commission or tribunal as is designated or constituted under any Act of the parliament of Canada for the regulation or control of the business of railways.
We are referred to the Railway Commission Bill which is now before the House as the authority which shall control the rates over the Canadian Northern Railway. I have every confidence that it would be possible to provide a Bill that would control these rates, but I have looked at the provision contained in section 2G0 which. I presume, is the provision relating to the control of tariffs, and I do not find that, in my estimation, it meets the case or that it is intended to meet the case. If I understand the general purposes of the Railway Commission Bill it is that it shall prevent discrimination in rates, that it shall tend to the equalization of rates, that it shall provide against the conditions which prevail throughout Canada where one town is discriminated against in favour of another, or where certain differences are made by one railway from another. It is not the equalization of rates that we want. It is not equalization that we need. As I said a few moments ago, we need that the rates shall be cut to the bone, that we shall get the lowest rate which it is possible to get in order to transact our trade. The Railway Commission Bill does not contemplate any such action and under its provisions as they stand, it -would be impossible to take such action because it would be distinctly contrary to the spirit, and even to the letter of the Bill. Therefore, I say the Railway Commission Bill does not meet the case as w7e understand it. Our claim is that in consideration of special aid given, a special arrangement should be made in regard to rates. Such a condition is not contemplated in the railway commission. The position which I take is that at the time we are making this bargain with this company is the time when we shall agree upon the maximum rates which that company shall charge upon freight going out and coming in. That is the time to make the bargain and it is the only time to make it. We are giving them a definite amount of assistance for a definite purpose. It appears that we can hedge them around with conditions in regard to this, that and the other thing of minor importance, and now is the time to impose the conditions which are of the importance of life and death to the

country served and to this whole country.
It is not enough to say that the government even would control the rates. The government has control of rates over many railways in Canada, but I have never heard yet that the government exercised that control with regard to the amount of aid which was given to the railway in order to ensure its construction. I do not know' that it would he justified in doing so under the conditions under which aid was given. The only effective reduction of rates which we have had in the North-west Territories has been the reduction that was brought about by the Crow's Nest bargain when, in consideration of a sum of money paid, a specilic reduction of rates was given. That was a plain business proposition, and it was satisfactory as far as it went. I believe, still, that the railway company got a good deal the best of the bargain, but this country got something that it never would have got otherwise, and that is the only thing it has ever got out of the aid that it has given to railways. I do not wish to be unpleasant, but I will just draw the attention of the committee to a little incident in connection with the Crow's Nest Railway which would indicate why some of us have not the fullest confidence in the mere general control of rates by the government. Under the Crow's Nest bargain the government has the right to regulate the rates from point to point upon that piece of railway. After that road was put in operation a schedule of rates was put in force which was most unsatisfactory to the towns and villages along the railway. The people complained against that schedule. The complaint was voiced here in this House.
I am looking at the lion. Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) now, and he will remember that he told us that he had examined that schedule of rates and was satisfied that it was a fair schedule of rates. Not very many months after that the railway company reduced the rates so as to make them fairly satisfactory to the points served ? We looked to the government on that occasion to compel the railway company to reduce its rates and we were put in the position of having agreed to a bargain which as far as the public could see meant nothing as to the control of rates on an occasion when, that control should most certainly have been exercised. The fact that the company afterwards did reduce the rates shows that the rates were unreasonable. I do not wish to press the matter further at the present time, but as the representative of a part of the North-west Territories, and as the representative of a part of the country to be served by this proposed railway, I must say to the government and to this House that as far as the people there are concerned they will look with very great dissatisfaction upon the fact of large government assistance being given even to this
railway unless satisfactory conditions are made as to definite maximum rates along its line, so that it shall be apparent to the country at large that value in rates is being secured at the time the aid is being given.

Mr. Chairman, I do-not wish to say anything in reference to this Bill at present, but the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver) has made a statement with which I do not coincide in saying that Spokane was built up at the expense of British Columbia on account of high freight rates. I am going to ask him the distance between Spokane and the Kootenay, and the coast cities and the Kootenay. I may say that Spokane is fifty miles from the Kootenay country whereas the coast cities are 425 miles from it. Hon. gentlemen can easily see that it could not be on account of the difference in freight rates that Spokane has been built up at the expense of our country for the simple reason that there is no comparison to be made in that regard. It is rather because the people on the American side were more progressive and took possession of the land.
May I ask the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Macpherson) if he admits that Spokane has been built up largely by the trade of the Kootenay ?

No, I do not admit that at all. I say that Spokane has been built up largely on account of the gold and copper mines of the Kootenay. The people from the American side came over possessed themselves of the land which was there and built up Spokane from the profits of the mines. It was entirely because of the gold they took out of the country.

I would like to say in regard to freight rates that Spokane is not an originator of traffic. It is not a manufacturing city nor a city built on commerce. Its supplies have to be brought by rail from ocean ports and from manufacturing centres. It is within, I believe, 150 miles of Nelson, which is the commercial centre of the Kootenay country. Nelson is just as close to the manufacturing centres from which Spokane draws its supplies as Spokane is, and if Spokane draws the trade rather than Nelson, it is because Spokane has better freight rates than Nelson, and we are here to see that Nelson gets as good freight rates as Spokane when the opportunity arises.
On the second resolution,

What is the scheme of the second clause of the resolution ? Is it intended that there shall be a mortgage to a trustee which shall be security to the debenture holders as well as the guarantee of the government, or is it intended that there shall be a mortgage to the government, securing the govern-

ment against any loss consequent upon its guarantee of the bonds ? The resolution is rather indefinite as to that.

The proposal was that bonds should issue with a mortgage to a trustee, the bonds being endorsed by the government. Also there should be an additional mortgage upon the other portion of the company's system which are already encumbered to some extent, that would be a separate and independent instrument.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: There are two distinct things. One is a series of bonds guaranteed by the Crown. In passing, I may say that there should be some definition of the word ' government ' which is not a word known to the law, and in the Manitoba Act the word ' government,' although used in the statute, was defined in the first instance as meaning the Crown represented by the executive government in Manitoba, and I suppose that course will be pursued in this case. Now, you may have bonds guaranteed by the government and also secured by a mortgage to the trustee. That is one proposition. I would not suppose that very much additional value would be given to the bonds by mortgage over the line of railway, provided they are secured by a guarantee of the government, because in that way the credit of the whole country, including the railway and everything else, is pledged to the holders of the bonds for the time being. If we are to give the guarantee of the government, one would suppose the best course would be a mortgage to the government securing the government against any loss consequent upon the guarantee which it had given for the purpose of securing these bonds. There are two distinct methods of procedure, and I cannot quite understand from the second clause of the resolution which of those modes is proposed, though I would supppose, looking on it from a practical standpoint, that the latter one would be preferred by the government. What is really intended by the second clause ?

I stated that what was in the mind of the drafter of the resolution was that bonds should issue in the ordinary way, bearing the government guarantee, and that a mortgage should issue to the trustee or trustees, which should cover all the assets and property of the railway company as mentioned to secure these bonds.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I realize that a mortgage of that kind could be drawn in such a way as to be a security to the Crown, but it would require to contain provisions very different from those which are usually contained in a mortgage given to a trustee for the purpose of securing bonds on a railway.
Of course it would.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It must not only be for the benefit of the bondholders, but there must be elaborate provisions in it for the purpose of enabling the government to take advantage of any provisions of the mortgage upon default being made by the company, and upon the government paying any sums the company would otherwise be obliged to pay. May I ask the minister, whether or not the mortgage proposed to be taken has been drafted V
Not yet.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: It would have, perhaps, been more satisfactory to us if that had been before the House, so that we might understand the remedies which the government would have in such a case. The result of a default might be that the government might acquire the right to enter into possession of this railway.
That is what we would contemplate.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Of course, the ordinary form of mortgage would not at ail cover that.
No.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
It seems to me it might make some difference in the consideration of this proposition if the House knew exactly what the terms of the proposal were in that regard. The mortgage is one of the all important features in this connection. For example, to what extent must the company be in default in the payment of interest before the government can enter and take possession and operate the road as its own ? What remedies will the government have in that regard V What right would the company have in such a case to come in and redeem its property from the possession of the government. There are a great many interesting questions which would arise upon the consideration of the terms of the proposed mortgage, and if the Minister does not present to the [DOT] House a draft of the mortgage, he ought to be in a position to give us some outline of the provisions in that respect which the mortgage will contain when this transaction is carried through to a conclusion. Suppose the company should be in default of its interest for a number of years, during which the government is paying interest upon these bonds, when would the time come at which the government could take some proceedings for the purpose of enforcing against the railway repayment of the money which it has been obliged to advance on behalf of the company ; when do you reach the stage at which the govern-

ment shall have the power to enter into possession of the road and to operate it in such a way as to relieve itself from any such burden in the future ?

All these are matters of detail and they will have, of course, to be covered by any documents that are executed between the parties. We have fully in our minds that all these points and others must necessarily arise, when we are proceeding to draft the security which is to be given and held by the government, and which it would be perhaps unnecessary to anticipate at this stage. The resolutions are clear, we are providing that aid Shall be given in such a way, and shall be carried out by such instruments as will fully secure the government. At the same time, if the government should make any advances in respect of the interest defaulted by the company, or make any payment on account of the principal, we would necessarily step into the position of the original creditors or bondholders for the full amount we had paid. All these things have to be thought out very carefully, and I think it would not be wise for us hastily to draft the document in order to lay them before parliament. There need be no great hurry in framing the instrument. We will take all the time necessary in order that the public interests shall be fully safeguarded. I can quite understand that my hon. friend would wish it to be very carefully prepared ; but in order to this careful preparation, it is not essential that it should be done now. In fact, it would be difficult to have it prepared now with the care and deliberation with which a transaction of this kind ought to be managed. It must rest on the responsibility of the government entirely to see that the conditions under which parliament has granted the aid shall be observed. I think this a reasonable view to present to the committee, and I certainlv would be very loath to think that the committee or the House would desire to have all these minute details laid on the Table, and action with respect to the matter precipitated.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The hon. minister made some interesting remarks when viewed in connection with the remarks of the hon. member for Alberta (Mr. Oliver), who said that no doubt this $13,000 a mile would cover the entire cost of this road.
I have not expressed that opinion.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Alberta did so. The minister said that the government must take precautions to have a thorough security. I do not know that a security on your own property would be a good security ; I do not know that any money-lender would consider that good security for the money he was lending. This clause reads :
The said mortgage shall also form a charge next after the charges existing thereon.
You take a mortgage for part of the money only, and a second mortgage at that. We do not know how many preferred bonds may be on the property under the $10,000 agreement. Before we go any further, I think the contract and the map should be in the hands of the members of this House, if a proper contract is to be made. One reason for the strong feeling which is abroad in the country to-day against subsidies being given to railroads is that for a number of years past the subsidies given, with the small amount of bonded indebtedness added, have been sufficient to build all the roads that have been built, and the railway promoters have put in little or nothing. It is very easy for people to become millionaires if the money is put into their hands. I hope the minister will take the House into his confidence and let us have this contract before the matter is further gone into.

I will call my hon. friend's attention to the fact that his supposition that we were without knowledge of either the character or the amount of the prior securities on the other portion of the Northern system, is not well founded. Perhaps the hon. member was not present when I stated to the committee the facts in regard to that. If not, he will see them in 'Hansard ' to-morrow.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The hon. minister says that these are matters of detail. They are in one sense ; but they are matters of detail that depend on principle. For example, all that this clause provides is that the government shall have a first charge. The method of enforcing that charge, the time at which it shall be enforced. the consequences of enforcing it. are not dealt with. The provisions in that regard are not as definite as they were in the case of the Drummond Counties Railway, where the document itself was brought down, or in the case of the agreement with the Grand Trunk Railway.
We were purchasing a property, and we had come to an agreement, and we submitted to this House the agreement which had been arrived at.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: In the case of the Grand Trunk you were acquiring terminals. and were providing for some aid for the Victoria bridge.
We did not provide the aid in that document, but by a separate vote, as a separate proposition.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: Was there not an agreement submitted to the House in regard to that as well?
No, that was not part of the agreement.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CABALS.

speechtext: I know that it was not part of the agreement as to the terminals ; but was it not in an agreement by itself ?
No.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: The difficulty is that one seems hardly to be able fully to grasp the proposition when the clause is couched in such general terms as this. How is the House to judge accurately as to the future relations between the government and the company ? You have a clause which simply provides that there shall be a first charge, and the committee have nothing before it to show the conditions under which that charge can be enforced, or under which the government might be obliged at some future time to operate the railway. If the minister cannot place the mortgage before the House, can he not give us an outline of the policy or the scope of the proposed mortgage ? If any clause of the agreement is to stand. I would suggest that it Should be this one.

I have no objection to that if the hon. gentleman desires it; but I do not accede to the suggestion with any intention of conveying the impression to the mind of mv hon. friend that I think it would be desirable that precise statements should be made in respect to the matters he alludes to.
speakername: The MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS.

speechtext: I am speaking of an outline.

If I attempted to give an outline. it would be necessary for me to indicate with some definiteness what the proposals are to be. We think parliament ought to be willing to leave the working out of these proposals in our hands, on our responsibility. Of course, the question of responsibility arises anyway. We bring the proposals here on our responsibility, and the responsibility remains. Parliament has said, you may do so and so, you may make such and such arrangements with this company, safeguarding the public interests. After parliament has settled on this, we shall proceed to examine the question in all its bearings. It then becomes a matter of negotiation and discussion as to how and with what particular restrictions and regulations this arrangement is to be worked out. Take the question, which I have not been able to think about very much yet, as to when the government would be justified in exercising its power of retaking this property on default in the payment of interest, it is a very proper thing to consider in all its bearings as to whether a reasonable time might not be allowed to elapse before taking over Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
the road, and it would not be wise to say that such time shall be one, two or three years or more. Conditions might arise that would make it contrary to public interest to enforce this power and take possession. It must be for the government, with a knowledge of all the facts, to say, when a default takes place, whether it should enforce its power or not-whether it should or not allow the interest to accumulate and the company to operate the road. All these things are matters concerning which it would not be wise to make any definite statement because our future course must be guided by the circumstances.
