Before you leave the Chair, Mr. Speaker, I desire to call the attention of the House, and particularly of the government, to a matter of long standing, which seems to me has been now put off long enough, and should be settled for the sake of the good name of Canada. With the indulgence of the House, I shall speak for a few moments upon a matter which I can only class as a debt of honour. I can quite understand that the matter of the Chignecto Marine Transport Railway has become rather hackneyed in the last ten or fifteen years. But, while it may be hackneyed, so long as it is not settled, it remains a stain upon the honour of this country and an impediment in the way of those who desire to secure the investment of capital, particularly of British capital in this Dominion. The promoters of the Chignecto Marine Transport Railway have abandoned the construction of that railway. Therefore, I am not here to-night urging upon the government that they should vote a subsidy to this company, or that they should allow this company to proceed and complete the works, but I am

here to appeal to the government to settle with these people and so-to repeat the expression I have already used-wipe off a debt of honour of the Dominion of Canada. 1 do not propose to take up more time than is absolutely necessary in explaining this matter. In the first place, I wish to contend that the connecting of the waters of the Bay of Fundy and Northumberland straits was a matter decided not by one government alone, but by two governments at least. Away back as early as 1S25-to trace the history of this matter for a few moments- a survey of the Baie Verte canal to connect the waters of the St. Lawrence at Baie Yerte with the Bay of Fundy by cutting across the isthmus uniting Nova Scotia with New Brunswick was made by Mr. F. Hall. At a later date, about 1840. Mr. Thomas Telford, a civil engineer, revised the report of Mr. Hall upon the subject, and afterwards another report upon the same project was prepared by a royal engineer, Captain Crawley. I will not go into all the surveys and reports made upon this subject, but will come to the year 1870, when an Order in Council was passed by the government of that day, the government of Sir John Macdonald, appointing certain eminent engineers and others as a committee to investigate and report upon the proposed transportation facilities of the Dominion of Canada. That commission consisted of Mr. C. S. Gzowski, of Toronto ; Mr. D. D. Calvin, of Kingston ; Mr. George Laldlaw, of Toronto ; Sir Hugh Allan, of Montreal; Mr. Pierre Garneau, of Quebec ; Hon. William Stairs, of Halifax, and Mr. Alexander Jardine, of St. John. In the Order in Council, they were instructed to institute a thorough inquiry into the whole subject with all its bearings both in a commercial and engineering point of view, with the object of obtaining such reliable information as might furnish the necessary data on which to base a plan for the improvement of the canal system of the Dominion of a comprehensive character, and such as would enable Canada to compete with success for the transit trade of the great west ; and further to inquire with regard to a number of works and improvements, and among those works enumerated was the construction of the Baie Yerte canal across the isthmus dividing the Bay of Fundy from the gulf of St. Lawrence. And the commissioners were further instructed by this Order in Council to report as to the works and improvements which ought to, in their judgment, be constructed. On the 24th February, 1871, the commission submitted their report, which stated the following with reference to the Baie Verte canal :
Inseparably connected with the growth of the intercolonial trade is the construction of the Bay Verte canal, across the isthmus connecting the provinces of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. The advantages that must accrue, not merely to the Dominion as a whole, hut to the commerce cf the maritime provinces, are so
clearly pointed out by the Boards of Trade of all the leading cities of Canada and by men interested in the development of our commercial interests, not simply the merchants of St. John and other places in the locality of the proposed canal, but merchants of Hamilton, Toronto, Ottawa and Quebec, that it is superfluous for the commissioners to do more than briefly refer to a few salient features of the scheme.
A steamer laden with flour for St. John, N.B., now goes down the gulf as far as Shediac where the cargo is transported by rail to its destination. The total distance by water from Shediae through the gut of Canso and around the coast of Nova Scotia to the Bay of Fundy as far as the commercial capital of New Brunswick is about 600 miles, and the consequence is that there is little or no direct communication between the Bay of Fundy ports and those of the River St. Lawrence. By a canal through the isthmus the distance from Shediac to St. John will not be much more than 100 miles.
This fact will show the insuperable obstacle that now exists to anything like extensive commerce between Montreal and the Bay of Fundy ports of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia and the great impulse which must be necessarily given to trade by the opening up of a route which will shorten distance so considerably, furnish an inland navigation from the lakes to Boston, and consequently lessen freight between these points at least 25 per cent.
The report then goes on to show all the interests of the maritime provinces that would be benefited, particularly In the matter of the coal trade. The freight to Boston, they say, would be reduced at least $1 per ton. The lumber and fishery interests of the gulf of St. Lawrence, both of Prince Edward Island and what is generally known as the north shore of New Brunswick, will also be benefited equally with the coal trade of Pictou, by their being afforded a safer and shorter route, not only to the ports of the Bay of Fundy, but also to those of the north-western coast of the United States.
These distinguished men discussed the benefits of the construction of the Bay of Fundy canal. They referred to the great importance it would be, not only to the provinces down by the sea, but to the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. They then conclude by referring to the great impulse it will give to the ship-building and carrying trade of the Dominion generally. In their report they classify the relative importance of the several public works which are under their eye, and the proposed improvements to which their attention has been directed, and they recommended these works in the order in which they should be proceeded with. In this plan they divided the works into four separate classes, and in the first class they placed the construction of the Bay Verte canal. In the report on the engineering aspects, I find the following :
The evidence submitted points out with remarkable force and unanimity the necessity of opening a highway for commerce between the gulf of the St. Lawrence and the head waters of the Bay of Fundy through the Isthmus of Chigneeto, dividing them.

And submitting a report of Mr. Keefer, C. E., endorsed 'by Mr. Gzowski, they said :
We think this will remove all doubt as to the practicability of the proposed undertaking.
Now, Mr. Speaker, after that report had been submitted, the then government of the day voted certain sums of money for the construction of this work, as they classed it, of first class importance. The Mackenzie government coming into power, took this up and voted in one year the sum of $1,000,000 to connect the waters of Northumberland Straits with the Bay of Fundy. They had an engineer make more exhaustive reports. Mr. Mackenzie stated in the House that if that canal could be built for $5,000,000 he was quite willing to expend that amount of money, and towards that purpose he voted $1,000,000. It was found afterwards by a more careful examination by engineers that the work would cost, not $5,000,000, but probably between $9,000,000 and $10,000,000, and that amount rather staggered the project. They said they could not afford to spend so large a sum of money even upon so important a work-.
Now I want to point out that the government of Canada at that time was quite willing to expend $5,000,000 to connect the waters of the Northumberland Straits and those of the Bay of Fundy. The matter then lay quiescent until a Canadian engineer named Ketchum, eminent in his profession, came forward and said to the government of Canada :	You want to connect
these waters, you are willing to pay $5,000,000, you say, but you cannot afford to pay $10,000,000. I will build a ship railway across this Isthmus connecting these two waters, and it will cost you very much less than to construct a canal. Mr. Ketehuln's scheme was submitted to the government, it was endorsed and approved by the chief engineer of Railways and Canals in his report dated February 4, 1882. A company of Canadians was incorporated; and I am going to try to show that this scheme was concocted by Canadians, that Canadians went to London with the charter granted by the parliament of Canada, and secured the money which was spent upon this undertaking, and that money was lost by the British investors through what I consider the fault of the government and parliament of Canada. This company of Canadians, then, was incorporated. They did not have any money to spend upon the ship railway, and it was never supposed they would spend money upon a ship railway, they were simply a legal entity. They approached the parliament of Canada for certain legislation. Now, Sir, in 1882 the parliament of Canada passed two Acts, one incorporating this Canadian company and another granting a subsidy of $150,000 per year for twenty-five years. I want to call your attention to the words in the subsidy Act :
In consideration of the great advantages which would accrue to the maritime provinces Mr. LOGAN.
and the intercolonial trade of Canada generally from the construction of a ship railway across
the Isthmus of Chigneeto
What was the subsection ?
What year was that in ?

That was in 1894. In October, 1894, Mr. George E. Foster -went to London. A deputation of the Chignecto people waited on him and he made the following statement to them :
The government, however, in this matter is bound to take in other considerations than those of strict and absolute legality, and I caff assure you-and that is as far as I can go in an assurance as a responsible member of the government-that the government will take this matter up as was promised Mr. Provand, and we will

give it our best consideration on the grounds ot' what might be called moral obligations-of how it may affect credit, and also as we are primarily bound to do. in respect to the best interests of our own people, for whom we are trustees, and for whom we are bound to act with great care and prudence.
I think you are perfectly right in asking that you should have a decision upon this question as soon as possible. It has been impossible, and I may say it is impossible, to have a question of this gravity considered without what we call a full meeting of Council, and circumstances during the holidays have rendered it impossible for the government to be assembled in force. As you know, Sir John Thompson is coming to London for a few weeks, and as soon as he returns I have no doubt at all that the government will take the matter up and dispose of it so that you may, I think, confidently look for an answer to this question some where about the middle of December.
That was in 3S94, nine years ago. Shortly after that Sir John Thompson died at Windsor. In May, 1895, Mr. Provand' was summoned to Ottawa by cable from one of the ministers. He received a letter from Mr. Foster, then Minister of Finance at Ottawa, as follows:
Minister of Finance,
Ottawa, Canada,
May 29, 1895.
Dear Mr. Provand,-In pursuance of your conversation this morning in reference to the application made by you for an extension of time for the completion of the Chignecto Marine Railway, I beg to write you as follows :-The government has listened carefully to the presentation of the case of the company made by you, and, while disposed to attach all responsible weight to the reasons adduced for an extension of time, find it difficult under the present circumstances when every effort is being made to strengthen the financial position cf Canada by cutting off appropriations and refusing to enter into further obligations, to give a conclusive answer at present. The government will, however, take up your case for final disposition next year, and you may consider that the consequent delay does not in anv way imply an unfavourable view of the company's claims, and is entirely without prejudice to their further consideration.
Yours faithfully,
(Signed) GEORGE E. FOSTER.
Wliat year was that in ?	*

That was in 1895. Early in 1896 the government of the day agreed, as I understand it, to pass an Act during the approaching session revoting the subsidy. A private Bill was introduced into this House in 1896 to extend the time of the charter. This private Bill was defeated by a snap vote, so-called by one majority, but it was replaced on the order paper by a majority of seventeen. On account of the celebrated debate upon the school question that session, that parliament closed without the question again being taken up, and since that time. Mr. Speaker, to make a long story short, the company have been knocking at the doors of the parliament of
Canada asking for some redress for the condition of affairs in which they have found themselves. They claim that they were led into it to a very large extent by the Dominion government, by the high commissioner of Canada in England, and by the cabinet ministers of the day. I contend that the Canadian government were largely responsible for the promotion of this railway. It was first decided that it was necessary to connect the waters ; secondly, it was decided that it was too expensive to build a canal ; thirdly, Mr. Ketchum came forward with bis Canadian company and asked the government of Canada to give them a charter. That charter was given to them and they went to England, and British investors put their capital into this scheme. Mr. Speaker, I do not think that the people of this country know that there has been sunk in that railway, British capital to the extent of over $4,000,000. Sir Richard Cartwright now the Minister of Trade and Commerce, made the following statement in parliament :
. The fact of parliament granting a subsdy of $170,000 a year for twenty years to this railway will imply to the minds of English capitalists, from whose pockets I take it that this money is expected, that the Canadian government have looked into the work, that they believe it to be a valuable work, and that it may fairly be implied that the government believe it to be reasonably profitable to those people whose money we are practically securing in consequence of our having granted a subsidy.
Sir Charles Tupper, Bart, then High Commissioner, when a deputation waited on him in London said :
In the light of all that has occurred, in the light of my thorough knowledge and familiarity with the sections of the country through which this railway is to run, and with my knowledge of the commercial business and shipping trade of Canada, I have no hesitation in saying I believe to-day that all that is required is the capital to be forthcoming to complete this undertaking to make it not only a thorough engineering but an equally great financial success, and that the return the parties supplying th^ capital may confidently look forward to W placed as much, in my judgment, beyond doubt, in connection with the subsidy which is provided by the government of Canada, as an. financial undertaking or business enterprise that was ever presented to the public.
That is what the High Commissioner for Canada, speaking to these investors said: and after they had put $4,000,000 of then money into this enterprise, these people approaching him as the representative of Canada,' were told that it was as good an investment as any financial undertaking or business enterprise that was ever presented to the public. And upon the statements formerly made by the High Commissioner of Canada, representing Canada as he did, the English investors poured their money into this enterprise, and yet, Sir, when they afterwards were caught by the amendment to the Railway Act; when they were not able to issue their debentures at a time
Would the hon. gentleman be kind* enough to give me the year that Sir Richard Cartwright made that speech which has been quoted ?

I cannot give the exact date, but I quoted it from ' Hansard.' These investors in the ship railway had another interview with Sir Charles Tupper and replying to them on the 20th of March, 1893, he said :	[DOT]
There is no doubt whatever that the parties who have invested their money in this enterprise are in a position to claim from the government of Canada, in my opinion, the fullest and fairest consideration. They have entered upon this measure upon no imperfect calculations. Every means that were possible that could be taken to warrant the enterprise being presented to capitalists as a sound enterprise were taken.
And as to thq extension of time to complete the railway he said :
Now, it is not necessary to dwell more upon that unfortunate and untoward event that has brought this work to a standstill ; but I am afraid you cannot expect the government of Canada to do more than they have set forth in the Order in Council-that is to say, that when, as you have rightly said, it is not usual for governments or anybody else to expect contractors-especially in connection with very great undertakings-to complete them at the time-and I know of no instance in which any government or any respectable concern of any kind have ever taken advantage of the stoppage of the work, from circumstances altogether beyond the control of the parties, for the purpose of relieving themselves of any responsibility. I do not believe the government of Canada will do so. I do not believe it. I believe not only their sense of right and of justice to the promoters and capitalists connected with the great enterprise, but their regard for the financial standing and character of the country itself, will ensure to you that, if at an early period you are in a position to comply with the terms of the Order in Council, you will find a fair and reasonable extension of the time necessary to complete the work. I have great pleasure in saying that to you, because I feel you are entitled to that consideration, and I am sure it will not be withheld by the government of Canada.
I could quote at considerable length, Mr. Speaker, the opinions of Canadian newspapers on this Chignecto Marine Transport Railway matter, but I shall select only a few. Take the following from the Toronto ' Globe,' which said :
The question more immediately concerning the Canadian people is to what extent the Dominion government is liable. It is true that the promise of a twenty years' subsidy was conditional on the completion of the work, but it is equally obvious that the action of parliament was the bait which caught the British investor, who would not have bitten at a naked hook. The original subsidy promised in 1882 was for $150,000 a year for twenty-five years, but in 1886 this was changed to a subsidy of $170,000 a year for twenty years. If we repudiate all responsibility, as technically we should be warranted in doing, the credit of the Dominion would suffer, for there can be no doubt that we have incurred a considerable degree of moral responsibility in connection with the undertaking.
The following is from the Ottawa Daily ' Free Press,' which says :
But there is an aspect of the ease which is almost painful, as it practically amounts to a rational disgrace. On the strength of the en-dorsation given it by governmental and parliamentary procedure, many people in Britain have been induced to sink money in the project whisk must now be regarded as lost.
Mr. Provand addressed a meeting of senators in Ottawa, and the proceedings were reported in the Ottawa ' Evening Journal ' of the following day, from which I quote. When he had finished his address, Sir Mackenzie Bowell, who was Prime Minister in the last administration, said :
Mr. Provand did not claim he had any legal right, but put his claim on moral and equitable grounds, and on the ground that all other subsidized enterprises, except this one, had been

given renewals when they failed to carry out their work in the first instance. He knew of no other company than the Ship Railway Company hut had been treated otherwise. Mr. Pro-vand's position was 1 treat us as you have treated others, otherwise give us compensation.' He claimed the investors had looked at the Acts of parliament, and seeing that they were ensured so much, had therefore put their money into the project.
1 will quote what was said by the Hon. Sir John Abbott, then Prime Minister, in the debate which took place on the application for the renewal of this charter :
It seems to me that we are to a great degree bound in good faith to give these contractors the opportunity of completing this work. I do not see very well how we could refuse them. I ihink a refusal to allow men who have spent three millions of dollars to spend $1,500,000 more would work very unfortunately on our enterprises, when we apply to England to borrow money.to finish them with, and I think it would be an extremely hard measure to mete out to these contractors to say that, not having completed their work within the precise time mentioned in the contract, they should be mulct of so large a sum as they have invested in it.
I will not quote any more from newspapers or from the speeches of public men of Canada. The company are asking, as they have been for the last ten years, for compensation. They claim that they are not being fairly treated. They claim that other companies have been given instructions to build certain works in Canada in a semipartnership with the Dominion government, and that these companies have been compensated when they had not an opportunity of completing their contract. This company claim that they were partners of the Dominion government in connecting the waters of the Bay of Fundy with those of the Northumberland straits, and thus carrying out the project of the commission which I had quoted in the first part of my remarks. They come and ask that, as they were led into this undertaking by the action of parliament and its agent, they be compensated to some extent for the loss they have sustained.
Apart from that phase of the subject altogether, the Chignecto Ship Railway bonds and other securities are to-day spread among the whole investing public of Great Britain. I have a list here of about thirty hanking institutions which hold Chignecto Ship Railway bonds and shares, including the London and Westminster Bank; Balli and Sons (Greek bankers); Capital and Counties Bank; Martins Bank, Limited;; Prescotts Bunk; Union Bank; Union Bank of Scotland; Cocks, Biddulph and Company; Manchester and County Bank; Coutts and Company; Lacond, Youall and Company; National Bank, Limited; and so on. Nearly every great financial institution in London hold the bonds and shares of this unfortunate company. Do you not think. Sir, that it is against the best interests of Canada that this matter should remain unsettled ? If the government of Mr. LOGAN.
Canada can see its way clear to come to a reasonable settlement with these people, it will certainly do us good in the financial markets of Great Britain. Those who have visited London know that you meet this matter whenever you talk to financial men over there. They refer to the bad treatment that was meted out to the Chignecto Ship Railway people; and when you place before them a Canadian proposition for the investment of their money, they point you to the history of that company, and say : That is the way you treated one British company; you got our money by representations, and then you refused to extend the time, and afterwards refused to compensate us for the money we expended. Apart from other phases of the subject, do you not think, Mr. Speaker, that it would pay the Dominion of Canada in the long run to settle this matter once and for ail, and remove it as a stain from the financial credit of the country ?
The company have spent, as I said, about $4,000,000. They do not ask for the return of all that'money, by any means. I am told by the representative of the company that they have paid in freights and in customs duties into the treasury of Canada about $500,000. Are we going to keep that money which these people have given us to bring in the machinery for the construction of their railway ? They ask first for reasonable compensation for the large expenditure they have made. They did not default in the payment of their men. The work happens to be in the county of Cumberland, which I represent. It does not make any difference to me politically what is done with this company; but I am here to plead with the government to treat these people in such a way as will remove the difficulties which exist between the company and the government and in the financial markets of England. *
There is one other consideration in this matter. In settling with this company, the government will also be settling a debt of honour to the county of Cumberland. That county, of course, anxious to secure the operation of this railway within its borders, granted the company a free right of way, for which the people bought the land and borrowed the money, taxing themselves to do so. They ask that if any settlement is made between the government and the company, it be arranged that this right of way, which was given for a specific purpose that has not been carried out, and which is not of any value to the railway people, they having abandoned the project, shall be returned to the county of Cumberland. Let me repeat that the company are not asking for any extension of time, as they have abandoned the project altogether; but they are throwing themselves on the mercy of Canada, and are asking the government of Canada to wipe out what we must all regard as a national debt of honour.

Some years ago, wlien I was In London I was asked to meet two gentlemen. I did so, and I found that they were trustees for the Chigneeto Ship Railway bondholders. I knew very little about that project further than what I had seen occasionally in the newspapers; but they explained the position of affairs to me, gave me the history of the company, told me how they had been induced to invest money in it, and asked me if I did not think they had a just and fail-claim on the government for a return of their money or for substantial compensation. The case as they put it before me interested me, and on my return to Canada, and after I became a member of this House, a year afterwards, I looked into the origin of this scheme, and I found that, as far as I could judge, there was a practically unanimous approval of the scheme by the parliament of Canada, not only when the Conservatives were in power, but when the late Hon. Alexander Mackenzie was at the head of the government. There was a curious unanimity in favour of the scheme by eminent engineers, and it was endorsed apparently by the business men of the country. At all events it was endorsed very strongly 'by the business men of the lower provinces, who ought to have known what its value was commercially. The result was that a company was formed, and parties went to England from this side and pressed on English investors the soundness of the scheme and the substantial aid which the Dominion government were giving to it; and a large amount of capital was raised. The hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) has gone into the details very* fully, giving the dates, and stating the various stages through which the company passed, so that I need not refer to these.
The company spent altogether about $4,000,000. Through a notorious misadventure on their part, they overlooked a clause in the Government Act which provided that they should spend 23 per cent of the capital subscribed before borrowing on the market. This prevented their raising the money. The money, however, required to complete the scheme was practically raised, and but for the financial crash of the Barings and those associated with that large firm, this scheme would have been completed and this government would have been bound to pay 8170,000 per year for twenty or twenty-five years. I told the trustees that in my judgment the scheme was a wild and visionary one, and that X would not advise the government, in any shape or way, to grant a furtherance of that subsidy on their completing the work, but it is clear that the government and these gentlemen who put their money into this scheme were practically in partnership, because these gentlemen were to obtain no return until the work was completed, and the government were under no obligation until the work was done.
Therefore, it was a question of mutual good faith. These men went on in good faith, but because of a financial panic they were unable to complete their scheme when practically three-fourths of the work was done. Had the government extended their charter -and I suppose that no extension is ever refused where substantial work is done- they would have been entitled to the subsidy, and I think that it is clearly a breech of faith on the part of the country to refuse to recognize the obligation the country is under to pay back, to some extent, at all events, to these men the money they have put into this enterprise. Looking at it as business men, we all wonder how it was possible such a scheme could have been inaugurated and backed up by our leading engineers, politicians and business men, still they apparently thought it would be a paying transaction and a substantial advantage to that particular section of the country. The scheme, I believe, would have been a failure, had it been completed.
At this point the electric lights went out, and the hon. member was unable, for a few minutes, to proceed with his remarks.
Mr. OSLE1L Mr. Speaker, if I were personally interested in this matter, and of a superstitious nature, I might take the sudden going out of these lights as rather an ill-augury of the cause which I am now arguing. But I rather take it as an indication that this House, recognizing that the transaction all round has been a bad job for the government and for the people of Canada, and for the men who put their money into it, will return to these bondholders a fair proportion of the money they have spent, will close out the transaction and have no more to do with it, and will try to avoid such transactions in the future.
I do really appeal earnestly to the government to consider this matter. I believe the country is morally bound to meet these bondholders, and, at all events, return them some proportion of the money that they have, in good faith, put into this scheme. This scheme was presented to the British public asking for their money with the practical endorsation of the Dominion of Canada, the endorsation of the engineers of the government, with the endorsation of leading men on both sides of the House, with the assurance of business men that the transaction would be a profitable and paying one. I do not know of any scheme that has been so thoroughly backed up in this manner and has been so thoroughly forced upon the English people as a scheme in which they could invest their money safely. And, I think this government will only be doing their duty and I believe the country will approve too of their action if they deal liberally with these bondholders and give them some compensation for the money they have lost.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. ISRAEL TARTE (Montreal, St. Mary's).
speechtext: I happen to have had the opportunity to study the question now before us when I had the honour of being a member of the government. Mr. Provand has come to Ottawa every year, I think, for the last five or six years. I was a member of the sub-committee to which the question was referred. The facts of the case are very simple. A company was organized to build the Chignecto Marine Railway. They were business men, and they undertook to carry out the work for a subsidy, agreeing that the subsidy should be payable when the work was completed. That is the basis of the whole agreement. X do not know whether my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Osier) has given attention to that part of the question.
I have ?

The company entered upon the work, but they were not very successful. They applied for an extension of time. Extensions were given to them twice. The last time when the government took up the matter was in 1896. I was then a member of the House. . Sir Charles Tupper, who was Prime Minister, was favourable to the undertaking. A private Bill was introduced. However, he did not make it a government measure. I do not remember exactly by whom the Bill was introduced into the House, but Sir Charles Tupper approved of it. However, there was such a strong opposition on the government benches that the Bill had to be given up and the charter was not renewed. Although no subsidy was then asked the opposition I say again, was so strong, that the charter, which was asked to be renewed on a private Bill was not then renewed. When we came into office the question was presented to us as to what should be done. Well, nothing was done, and the matter stands as it stood when Sir Charles Tupper left office. My hon. friend (Mr. Osier) said that these gentlemen from London were entitled to compensation. If the government make up their minds that it is in the interest of the country to pay these bondholders a sum of money, the government, of course, will be held responsible for the position they take. There is no legal ground for the claim. My hon. friend from Cumberland (Mr. Logan) has quoted from the speech of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright). I feel sure that if my hon. friend had read a little further down or a little further up in the speech, he would have found that his quotation does not at all render or do justice to the views of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. There was a strong debate in the House in 1896. There were several debates before that. I remember them very well, because I was then a member of the press. On every occasion, the Liberal party, which

was then in opposition opposed and denounced the scheme. As to that, there can be no doubt; ' Hansard ' is there to be appealed to. There was not a member of the Liberal party in the House that stood for the renewal of the charter. And, in 1896, the opposition on the government benches was so strong that the charter was not renewed. Why was it not renewed ? Because the scheme that, for a time, had been looked upon as a feasible scheme, was in those years looked upon as a fake, an impossible thing. The position in 1896 was exactly what I stated. The government considered that the scheme was not feasible, and that it would be a dangerous thing to renew the charter, as it would encourage men in the attempt to carrying out of a hopeless undertaking. These gentlemen failed in their undertaking. I am very sorry for them. But they were business men. It seems to me that the extension of their charter on two occasions was quite a sufficient measure at the hands of parliament to justify us, at any rate, to have some doubts as to the morality of their claims. They have failed as many other business men have failed in their undertaking. Now, if my hon. friend the Minister of Finance believes it necessary for Canadian credit to compensate these men, why, he is the Minister of Finance and it is for them to decide. But, on the ground of right, I do not think these gentlemen have any claim upon us. Whether the credit of this country can be impaired by our refusal to satisfy the claims presented to us, is another question.

I have listened very care'fully to the remarks made on both sides on this question. I know none of the parties, have never heard the names even of the bondholders in this matter. Two years ago I had the papers relating to it placed in my hands and I read them very carefully to form an opinion for myself of what was due from this country, if anything, to the people who had invested money in this unfortunate undertaking. The facts, as I understand them are briefly these :-About thirty years ago many prominent gentlemen in this Dominion conceived the idea that a canal or a ship railway at Chignecto would be a most valuable improvement, of the utmost importance to the provinces down by the sea. It was not a question of one political party or the other taking up that venture. Prominent men on both sides of politics, gentlemen who are in the ministry to-day and gentlemen who were in the ministry that preceded it, all seemed to take a m st favourable view of the propriety and necessity of proceeding with this work. For some reason or other, for several years nothing was done. It appeared that there were doubts about the estimates of the cost of the work. But. ultimately, a charter was obtained and

the work was undertaken. The Dominion parliament subsidized that work, agreeing to grant a very substantial aid to the undertaking. The work proceeded; the directors of the company, assisted by expressions of opinion from the highest men in the land, both in parliament and out of parliament, succeeded in obtaining a large amount of capital in England. There had been delay, the bonds that the company expected to issue were rendered impossible of issue owing to what I think everybody subsequently agreed was a stupid provision put into a clause of the Railway Act with regard to the issuing of bonds. This impeded the financial end of the undertaking for some time but ultimately the money was raised in England, a large sum of several million dollars.
Now there is one material feature in this matter X would like to call attention to. These bonds were not placed in England in the ordinary way, at a discount. I believe that every bond was placed there at par or above par. It was looked upon as a thoroughly legitimate undertaking, fostered and endorsed by the highest men of this Dominion and by parliament. Well, after that the work went on, and as we all know now, the undertaking proved a failure, a most disastrous one for every body connected with it. It was a huge blunder from beginning to end. The people in England who placed several millions of money in it were led to do so by assurances from people on this side, and every dollar that they expended in that way, might as well, and perhaps better have been thrown into the sea. Now as to the subsidy. After we agreed to give aid it was found that this undertaking was going to be a failure, that it would be better for all concerned if it had never been begun, and it was no use to expend another dollar upon it. The people connected with it wished to get an opportunity to go on with the work. The parliament of Canada, very rightly, I think, determined they would not extend the time for its completion. The result of that was that this Dominion saved the whole of the subsidy that we had agreed to give to these people. I do not mean to say that the parliament of Canada in those days refused to extend the time in order to get rid of paying that subsidy. But even if it had, I do not know that it would have been improper. I have only to say it was a reasonable thing for parliament to do. There was no use throwing away all this money. The undertaking had become absolutely hopeless, and, therefore, this Dominion was quite justified in refusing to give the company an extension of time to earn their subsidy.
But there arises another question. By refusing to extend the time for the construction of this work, we happily were able to save a very large sum of money that we otherwise would have lost, while these un-139i
fortunate people who had put up their money lost every dollar of it. Now we were all partners together, as I look upon it. They had been induced to spend their money, and we had agreed to spend ours. By a fortunate bit of luck, the facts became known in time for us to save our money, though too late for them * to save theirs. That is the whole position. We are all in a sense partners together, and whsjt is decent for us to do in these conditions ? As I look upon this question as a representative of the people, I would vote to do here to-day that which I, as an honourable man, would think I ought to do under similar circumstances in a personal transaction. I think it would be discreditable for us to take advantage of the people who were practically our partners in this undertaking. We led them into it. It was not an ordinary undertaking. Public men, ministers of the Crown, gave certificates, gave statements in this House and elsewhere, leading these people to put up their money. They put it up and they lost every dollar of it, not only the principal, but every dollar of interest, and we have not paid out a cent. Now I say under these circumstances, Mr. Speaker, it is not a question of legal right, it is a question of what is honourable and decent for this Dominion to do. I say the Dominion should do just what any hon. man in this House would do with a fellow man he was dealing with under like conditions. I do not know how much these gentlemen spent, some $4,000,000 are said to have been spent. I do not know whether that is the amount they expended or not, but the government can easily ascertain.
I say that in my humble judgment it would be a right and proper thing for the government of Canada to give some relief, to look at all these facts, all the circumstances, and to do what is right, to do what is generous, and to do what is even liberal, without ex travagance. For my part, I should be very glad to endorse such a course on the part of a Liberal ministry.

I think all the circumstances connected with this unfortunate transaction have been fully explained, .so that the members of the House who were not members at the time this transaction was going through, are fully informed of the circumstances. I heartily endorse the proposition that some arrangement should be made with these gentlemen who have put their money into this undertaking and lost it. All those who were in the Llouse and heard these matters discussed on the different occasions when they came up, will remember that it was not only one government, but two governments, the government of Mr. Mackenzie and the succeeding Conservative government, who endorsed this proposition. More than that, the government engineers at these different times also expressed, in writing, and re-

ports to the government, very strong representations that this would certainly be a successful and strong financial enterprise.
I attach more importance to the reports of our own officials than to any other representations that were made. All parties in this House agreed in what was done. I attribute the failure of the undertaking more to the evolution in railways, and their improvement in capacity and in cheapness of rates, than to any other reason. It is evident that the engineers and business and public men of those days were mistaken in their expectations. I go strongly with the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker), who has so well expressed the views I entertain. It was not because we did not wish to extend the time in the usual way, but because the House was so well satisfied that it was useless, that it would be a waste of money. If any hon. gentleman here will turn up the debates on that occasion when the extension of time was refused, he will find the speeches from the members of the lower provinces generally who were better informed, and better capable of judging than those of us from Ontario and Quebec.
The members, especially from the lower provinces generally, who were better informed and better capable of judging than those of us from Ontario and the west, satisfied me, at all events, that it was useless. While I felt that, still, I voted on the principle of the thing to extend it according to the ordinary usage. I did that for the purpose of keeping faith, while perfectly agreeing with the arguments that had "been presented that it would be entirely useless. The members of this House were satisfied that it would be useless to put more money into that unfortunate scheme because the evolution of circumstances and of development satisfied the good sense of the House that what had been done was a mistake. Fortunately for those who were in favour of the government doing something for this company, both political parties were committed to that judgment as to the futility of the work and I think that ought to have a very strong influence in regard to the settlement of this affair. Even the promoters of the scheme themselves who put-up their money are not appealing to us here to say that it would have been well for the country or for themselves if they had been given an opportunity of fully expending the subsidy. They would be better satisfied to make some fair arrangement now than if we had expended more money than we did in assisting them and obliging them to complete the work, and it would be more satisfactory to the country than if the government were obliged to ask parliament'for this large subsidy which the people of this country have to pay. It is not a question of breach of faith on either side, but, under the circumstances, I think it is better, both for the people of this country and for the people who were so un-Hon. Mr. TISDALE.
fortunate as to invest their money in the enterprise and who had good reason to believe from the representations of the government and of the engineers of the government, that it would be a perfectly satisfactory security, that they were not permitted to complete the work and that the government was not called upon to pay the subsidy. I think the government could probably satisfy the claims of these people for less money than it -would have cost if we had extended the time and been called upon to pay the subsidy. That being the case IThink the government would do well to arrange with them. I can add my testimony to that of the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Osier) as to the impression that this transaction has created in England in connection with some matters that some friends of mine and myself have been endeavouring to negotiate in the old country. We commenced eight or ten years ago and the first influence we had to encounter was this Chignecto claim. I did not wonder at it when I heard of the list of banks that were interested in this unfortunate transaction. I am, therefore, as one of the representatives of the people of this country, prepared to take my share of the responsibility of asking the government to make some fair and satisfactory arrangement with these people in .respect of the matter and get it out of the way.

I have just a few words to say in reference to this matter. I was in the House when the Bill was introduced for the building of this Chignecto Railway, and we must all remember that this undertaking had the imprimatur of the parliament of Canada, of the engineers connected with the Railway Department as to the feasibility of it, and of the Minister of Railways and Canals responsible to the people who was looked upon as speaking authoritatively and witli knowledge by the financial men in England when, speaking as to the financial position of the undertaking, he stated in the best of good faith that there was every probability of the company being recouped for the money expended on it. We were first to give $150,000 a year, but the subsidy was afterwards increased to $170,000. By an oversight in amending the Railway Act. a provision was introduced which affected this Chignecto Railway when parliament had no intention of applying the amendment 1o that particular undertaking at all, which rendered it impossible for the parties who were interested in this scheme to raise the money for the purpose of building the work. This amendment required the expenditure of 20 per cent of the capital before the company could float their bonds. However, afterwards, when that was remedied by parliament, and when they were in a position to put bonds upon the market, the unfortunate financial crisis occurred which caused J the failure of Baring Bros, and rendered

it impossible for any scheme, no matter how good it was, to obtain money on the English market. Now, are we to take advantage of tiie unfortunate position of the parties who invested their money in this undertaking in good faith ? It has been said that we have no legal obligation. We do not keep ourselves strictly in this House to legal obligation. Time and again we have eliminated the legal responsibility in submitting questions for damages to the court and we have left the court virtually to judge as to the moral obligations of the people of this country. I contend, first, that we have a moral obligation to these people who invested their money in the undertaking. They did it on the faith of parliament, on the statement of lending men of this country, they did it on the statement of the engineers attached to the Department of Railways and Canals, and in addition they submitted the question to the first engineers in Great Britain. The gentleman who was the architect of the bridge across the Frith of Forth, the foremost engineer in Great Britain, reported favourably as to the feasibility of the scheme. It is true we changed our minds afterwards. It is true, as stated by the hon. ex-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) that the opposition at .that time were to a man opposed to the scheme. They opposed the proposal to renew the charter in 1896. Sir Charles Tapper, if he had remained in the government of this country, would have brought down a measure for the purpose, to a certain extent, of indemnifying these people for the money they had put into the undertaking. Whether they are entitled to the whole of it or whether they are entitled to only a share of it I will not say. but the penalty we attach to them is far in excess of their default. Why should they, because they were unable to raise the money, forfeit the whole amount of the money which they expended on the undertaking. We have all agreed now that there is no necessity for the building of this work. We have all agreed on both sides of the House that the undertaking shall not be built.
When did we make that discovery ?

The feeling in tlie country, as I judge from public opinion, is that an undertaking of that kind would not be a financial success and that the government would not be justified in the payment of the money necessary to carry it to a conclusion. What I am contending for is the moral obligation of the people to do something for the people who have invested their money on the imprimatur of this parliament, on the statement of the Minister of Railways and Canals, on the statement of the department which was responsible for the introduction of the measure providing for an undertaking which they believed would be a financial success. Admitting that they have no legal claim,
yet they come before the parliament of Canada in the same position as dozens of others who have been recouped for expenditures they made on the good faith of the support of the people of this country. I believe that the Minister of Finance would have almost the unanimous support of the people of Canada if he did something to compensate these people for the large sum of money they have expended on this undertaking. I believe that money so expended to show our good faith, would be worth more to us than the cash itself in establishing our good name before the world.

I have listened to my hon friend from Cumberland (Mr. Logan) who gave a detailed history of this unfortunate enterprise. I have also listened to my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) who diagnosed the matter very clearly, and I believe that we, as an honourable body, should look upou this matter as a party to the contract with the English investors who undertook the work. We wisely carried out our part of the contract and it was no fault of ours that the project failed, except that perhaps some may say that we deprived the company of the opportunity of continuing the work owing to a clause in the Railway Act passed subsequently. I hardly like to venture an opinion as to whether this was a proper enterprise or not, but I may say that I have visited the scene of the proposed shiprailway and I could not for the life of me understand how any engineer could ever have recommended such an undertaking. If I had a ship in the Northumberland Straits destined for Boston or New York, I would much prefer to have sent her by sea route rather than to take her over this ship-railway had it been built, even if I could have done so free of tolls. The tortuous waters of the Bay of Fundy would have been the greatest risk in the voyage, to say nothing of the dangers of the railway itself in putting a ship on a contrivance of that kind. However, that may be, it was an unfortunate enterprise, and under all the circumstances I feel satisfied that this parliament should in honour recoup those people for their losses, at least a part, more particularly as quite a number of the English investors were put to great sacrifices by the failure of the party to carry out this scheme. We may not be legally bound to recoup these people, but I certainly think we are morally bound. Even if we put it on the ground of it being a charitable act, but I want it to go to investors who put their money in it, not to stockbrokers, solicitors and adventurers. I, for one, would be prepared to advocate it. If the government does not consider that they should repay the whole of the money expended by them, then I would be in favour of letting them exercise their own discretion as to what they consider would be fair, or equitable, under the circumstances. This is not a party

question for both parties are involved. As I understand it, both the Mackenzie government and the Conservative government endorsed the project. When the company applied to have the charter extended, I felt as a member of this House, that it would be a charitable act to refuse the extension so that they might not he subject to further loss of money by this scheme. I felt that there was no use wasting more money in the continuation of that work. I fully endorse the position taken by the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) and others, and I trust that the government will consider the matter and do what is honourable and just in the premises.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (1-Ion. W.
S.	Fielding). I am afraid that I cannot go so far as some lion, gentlemen have in supporting the claims of this company, nor do I think they are quite correct in all the statements that have been made as to the circumstances under which this scheme was promoted. I may be wrong, but I think my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) is mistaken when he says that some members of the present administration supported the scheme. I do not remember whether there was a division on it in parliament.
There was in 1801.
I recollect that one member of the present administration took very strong ground against it, and Mr. Mackenzie also spoke in terms of hostility.
I have a distinct recollection of reading something signed by Sir Richard Cartwright in the very strongest terms referring to this.
In favour of the scheme ?
I think so.
Oh, no ; my hon. friend (Mr. Barker) is entirely mistaken. Sir Richard Cartwright condemned the scheme in the very strongest terms.
Hear, hear.
I think tlie member for South Norfolk (Hon. Mr. Tisdale) is not correct when he says that the scheme was supported by the Mackenzie government generally.
I think they endorsed it.
My hon. friend is mistaken. This particular scheme was not projected during the reign of the Mackenzie government.
Perhaps not.

There was a project for the construction of a canal, and when it was found that the cost Mr. KAULBACH.
of this canal was likely to lie very large the project was abandoned. However, I do not attach very much importance to that point. The government of Canada is a continuing body, and if any obligation in the name of Canada is incurred by1 one government the succeeding government is bound to carry out that obligation. I cannot think that there has been anything here to justify the charge of breach of faith. It is not contended that there is any legal obligation; if there were these gentlemen would have availed of the courts long since. Nor can I admit with the member for Cumberland that it is a debt of honour. If anything can be done for these unfortunate stock holders it must be done, not because they have a legal claim, not because they have even a moral claim, but as an act of grace and favour of this parliament irrespective of everything else.
Hon, Mr. TARTE. Hear, hear.

There has been some negotiations of late-I suppose it would be light to say there has never been a moment for some years that there have not been negotiations on the subject. It is now some twenty years since this scheme was first promoted, and it is some ten or eleven years since the scheme practically failed. According to the statement of my hon. friend from Cumberland, in 1892 application was made to the government of that day to restore the company to its former position. The government of the day did not do so; and although that Conservative government remained in power down to 1890, they never asked parliament to restore the company to its former position, for the reason stated by the hon. member for South Norfolk, that they and others had made up their minds that the scheme was not a wise one, and that it would not be well to continue it. That was the position when the present government came into power in 1896. This government took the ground that whatever might be said in favour of the scheme in earlier days- and I do not wish to go into tliat-it was now pretty well admitted by business men that the scheme was not a sound one, and therefore we felt that we should not give it a new lease of existence in order that other people might be induced to put money into it, and throw good money after bad. That left the question of compensation, and from that day to this that question has been pressed on the attention of the government; but up to a recent date the sums mentioned by the promoters of what they considered proper compensation were so very large that they did not seem to come within reasonable limits, and we did not feel like presenting the matter to parliament. I suppose this session would not be a constitutional one, if we had uot here our energetic friend who represents the company to press its claims. I do not know

that I can say more at present than that the matter is engaging the consideration of the government. Representations are being made to us by the agent of the English bondholders, and, in the light of the discussion that has taken place to-night, we will give the matter further consideration.

Motion agreed to, and House went into Committee of Supply.
Archives. $9,000.
What is the reason of the increase ?
This increase is largely in connection with the copying of French documents in Paris.
What is the nature of the increase ?

There is going on constantly in Paris an investigation into documents connected with early Canadian history. That work has been prosecuted very actively. This year a very large number of documents have been copied, and next year we expect that there will be more. A very long list of documents which have to be copied has been prepared for that purpose.
Is the increase owing entirely to that ?
Almost entirely.
Who is in charge of the work in Paris ?
Mr. Edouard Richard.
What do we pay him ?

$.1,000 a year, including expenses.
Collection anil compilation of criminal statistics. $1,800.
Who is the officer in charge of this work ?

Mr. George Johnson.
Statistical Year-book, $5,000.
What is the nature of the increase ?

The amount asked for is $1,000 more than last year, to provide for the printing of a larger number of copies, which have been asked for.
General statistics, $3,200.
What is that expenditure for this year ?

Some of the officers under Mr. Johnson are paid out of this vote. It is sometimes used
and sometimes not used, according to the exigencies of the work. The officers are sometimes engaged to work up particular statistics which are used in the compilation of the Year-book.
Is all this used in connection with the Year-book ?
Not always. I do not know of anything last year except in connection with the Year-book.
Has there been any special investigation ?
None during this current year.

I would like to ask the lion. Minister of Agriculture if any part of this sum has been paid for an examination of land values ? The hon. gentleman has had a Mr. Washington engaged for some time in connection with what are called general statistics, what has become of Mr. Washington's work ? Has the country the benefit of that long and painful examination he made of land values in the provinces, or has it been cast to one side ?
The report is laid on the Table. There is no other publication.
Does the hon. gentleman consider Mr. Washington's report of any value ?
Yes.
What does the hon. gentleman intend doing with it ?
It may be utilized when convenient.

It was shrewdly suspected that the hon. gentleman intended it for campaign literature, but after examination by himself and some other members of this House he became somewhat faint-hearted and doubted whether it would serve his purpose. Does he expect to be able to resurrect it in the future and turn it to account ? And what was the expenditure in connection with that report ?

The expenditure on the work was closed before the commencement of the current year, and there is no intention of renewing it in the ensuing year. I have not the details of that expenditure of two or three years ago available.
I presume that Mr. Washington is being provided for in some other way. Is that the case V
I am not aware of it.

The hon. minister was not aware of his having been employed on

a former occasion. He seemed to be taken by surprise when Mr. Washington made the statement before one of the committees last year that the minister had employed him. Mr. Washington was able to remind the hon. gentleman of some circumstances where there had been a conversation, in consequence of which Mr. Washington went down to the maritime provinces. Aid to agricultural societies, $7,000.

This is paid to the Agricultural Societies of the North-west Territories, and it is paid through the local government. This amount has been in the estimates during many years. It is paid to the individual societies 'who make a return of their membership, and each society gets an amount-based on its membership. The work of making that apportionment is left to the officers of the local government in the territories. The reason for this vote is that, in the provinces, the provincial governments deal with agricultural societies, but in view of the work to be done, this concession was made by the Dominion parliament.

I had occasion last year and on previous occasions to call attention to the very small sum expended fdr this purpose. The hon. gentleman states, that vote has been stationary for many years. Either agricultural societies must be unfairly dealt with or there is very little interest in matters of this kind in that country. In view of the large expenditure of the government, it seems to me that some explanation is due to the House as to why it is that, with such progress and development going on there, there is no greater increasing expenditure under this head.

Agricultural societies in the North-west Territories have not been increasing in number. The policy of the department there has been rather to centralize and amalgamate these societies. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Clancy) seems to think that enough money is not spent in the encouragement of agriculture in the North-west Territories. But when this vote was first introduced, this was the only agricultural work done in the Territories by the government. Since that time considerable other work has been undertaken, work in connection with the establishment of creamer-

ies, work in connection with live stock associations and the sending of speakers to farmers' institute meetings all over the Territories. In the opinion of the people there it was better to spend money in that kind of work rather than in agricultural societies. There has been no demand for the increase of this vote.
Are speakers sent from here to the North-west Territories to lecture to farmers ?
Speakers are arranged for to lecture before the institutes of the North-west Territories. Some are sent from here and some are arranged for in the territories.
Who are the parties sent from here ?

I have not a list of them at hand. That conies under another vote, and when that vote comes up, if the hon. gentleman wishes it, I will give the list. It will come up under vote for the branch commissioner of agriculture, &c., and also under experimental farms.

Fumigating stations, $3,500.
The country will look for some explanation as to the progress that is being made in that work and whether the hon. minister proposes to enlarge the operations.

There has been a slight enlargement of the operations. It was found that the station in British Columbia had to be kept open practically all winter, which involved extra expense. There was a larger number of passengers going through, and we have had to employ extra hands to do the work. I hen, again, I found that this year we were not able to pay all the bills out of the vote of this year. There may be something like $150 in the vote asked for to cover the arrearage, and make the ensuing year's expenditure all right.

Perhaps the hon. gentleman will explain to the committee wliat progress is being made for the purpose of arresting the ravages of the San Jos6 scale, and to prevent infected plants from coming into Canada, which I understand now undergo a process of fumigation.

My department has not undertaken in any way to try to stamp out the scale in this country, except that my officers, at the various horticultural and agricultural meetings, have explained the best methods of treating it. In the province of Ontario the local government have taken steps to try to stamp out the pest where it is in existence. The purpose of our government has been to prevent the importation of the pest into the country ; and I venture to say positively that in no case has an instance been found in Canada, since the passage of the Act under which this vote is administered, of the introduction of the San Josd scale from foreign countries. I think, therefore, we may congratulate ourselves that the action of parliament in passing that Act and in arranging for fumigation at certain ports, lias been successful. The work lias been canned out in such a way as to accomplish the object parliament had in passing the Act.
From what countries does fumigated stock come in ?

From the United States chiefly. The United States, Australia, Japan and the Hawaiian Islands are the places mentioned in the regulations and the Order in Council from which plants are prohibited without fumigation. Those are the countries which at present are known to be infested by this scale.
Is not tlie stock taken out of tlie boxes at tlie fumigating stations ?
Yes, it is unpacked from tlie boxes, put into a tight chamber and fumigated, and then repacked and sent on.
At what ports is it fumigated ?
The ports are Vancouver, Winnipeg, Windsor, Niagara Falls, St. John's, Quebec and St. John, New Brunswick.
Then stock coming into Nova Scotia has to come through St. John to be fumigated ?

Yes. There is only one port in the maritime provinces where they are fumigated. As a matter of fact our records show that nearly all the stock that comes into Nova Scotia comes from the United States. It has been suggested that a port should be established also in Nova Scotia, but on investigation into tlie actual facts of the trade, it did not seem to me that it would be justified by the amount of stock imported, which comes just as cheaply through tlie" port of St. John.

At that time the government declined to take it up, and relegated the matter to tlie provincial governments. Most, if not all, the provincial governments in Canada have taken part in arrangements for the Imperial Institute. They have not, however, maintained their exhibits in that high state of efficiency which seems to be necessary. with tlie dignity and importance of this country, and with its material resources. When in England a few years ago I came to the same conclusion, and discussed the matter with Lord Strathcona. Tracadie Lazaretto, $5,500.
Is this institution doing a useful work which warrants this vote every year ?

This is a work of absolute necessity. It was established before confederation, and was taken over by the Dominion government from the province of New Brunswick. The patients are not confined to the province of New Brunswick, and there are at present twenty patients. It is a curious fact that the number has varied very little for many years.
It has been stated in the press that a great number of them were Chinamen.

I do not think that there is a single Chinaman there, or that there has been. There are some in the Lazaretto in British Columbia, but that is not under my department. Most of the patients from Tracadie come from the lower provinces, but on one or two occasions lepers have been sent from the west.
Is it not the duty of the province to look after these lepers ?

I do not think there is any obligation on the Dominion to take charge of lepers except those in the maritime provinces. I will not speak positively as to the legal aspect of the question.
Public works-Health Act, $4,000.
What is this ?

Some years ago this parliament passed an Act for the purpose of protecting the health of employees on public works, by seeing that the employers provided proper sanitary arrangements for their employees, and especially in cases where there was no municipal organization. An inspector was appointed to see that the provisions of the Act were carried out, and his report appears in the annual report of my department.
Does that apply only to where there is no municipal or provincial organization ?
Speaking from memory, I think that the Act would cover places where there is a municipal organization, but where the employees are not living in the ordinary way, but are camping on the works.
